title: Rajiv Meherish, Founder of Dubai's Raju Omlet Chain, Dies at His UAE Home
excerpt: The Mumbai-born entrepreneur built a single-product egg restaurant into an eight-outlet chain studied by Harvard Business Review. He had lived in the UAE for over four decades.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Rajiv Meherish, founder of Raju Omlet, passed away on July 19, 2026.
  • He co-founded the restaurant chain in 2013, which grew to eight outlets.
  • Raju Omlet served over 80,000 eggs and 70,000 cups of tea monthly by 2023.
  • Meherish emphasized quality, sourcing fresh eggs at a premium price.
  • His son Nakul is expected to lead the brand's expansion into new markets.
  • Rajiv Meherish, the Indian-origin founder and CEO of Dubai restaurant chain Raju Omlet, passed away on Sunday, July 19, 2026.
  • Meherish co-founded the egg-focused eatery in 2013 with his son Nakul; the chain grew to eight outlets across the UAE and was featured in both a Harvard Business Review and an Ivey Business School case study.
  • A Mumbai University commerce graduate, Meherish spent over four decades in Dubai, working in media and publishing before turning to the restaurant business in his later years.
  • His son Nakul Meherish is expected to continue leading the brand, which had been planning expansion into Abu Dhabi and the wider GCC region.

Rajiv Meherish, the Indian-origin entrepreneur who built Dubai-based restaurant chain Raju Omlet into one of the UAE's most recognisable homegrown food brands, passed away on Sunday, according to multiple reports from Firstpost and Exchange4media. He was the founder and chief executive officer of the chain.

No cause of death was publicly disclosed at the time of reporting. Meherish, who had lived in the UAE for more than four decades, is survived by his son and business partner Nakul Meherish, who serves as the chain's owner and operator.

From Media Salesman to Restaurateur

A commerce postgraduate from Mumbai University, Meherish arrived in Dubai in 1980 and started as a salesman. From 1982, he spent nearly a decade selling advertising space for leading regional publications including Khaleej Times, Gulf News, and the Arabic-language daily Al Khaleej. After leaving the media business in 1989, he pivoted to publishing and events, working on projects with Dubai Duty Free, the Dubai Shopping Festival, Emirates Airlines, and government entities including Dubai Municipality and the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA).

The restaurant venture came much later. During a business trip to Vadodara, India, Meherish was taken by his taxi driver to a roadside egg handcart called Raju Omlet Centre, run by a cook named Rajesh Bhogilal Rana — known locally as Rajubhai. Though a vegetarian who had not eaten eggs for two decades, Meherish was persuaded to try an omelette. He was impressed enough to bring the concept to Dubai.

Building a Brand on Eggs

In June 2013, Meherish and Nakul opened the first Raju Omlet outlet — an 18-seat, 480-square-foot space in Al Karama, a neighbourhood with a large Indian expatriate population. The restaurant specialised in egg preparations served with Indian bread, priced between Dh10 and Dh22. A cup of chai cost Dh4.50.

Meherish's Business Philosophy
›Sourced fresh eggs daily, paying 30% premium.
›Maintained full salaries during COVID-19.
›Closed every Monday for staff rest.
›Provided competitive salaries and incentives.

"We only manage. Restaurants are run by sections of people — your staff and your customers. It is very essential to keep them happy, and then you can go home and count your monies."

— Rajiv Meherish

The father-son team built the brand through a distinctive radio advertising strategy. Rather than promoting the restaurant directly, the spots focused on the health benefits of eating eggs, airing during peak commuting hours. The approach drew academic attention: Raju Omlet became the subject of a case study published by Ivey Business School in 2015 and was later featured in a Harvard Business Review case study in 2016, which explored whether a single-product restaurant could sustain growth in a competitive market.

The chain expanded steadily. By its tenth anniversary in 2023, Raju Omlet had grown to eight branches across Dubai and Sharjah, serving over 80,000 eggs and 70,000 cups of tea per month. The menu, which began with just nine dishes, had expanded to 85 items, though eggs remained the centrepiece. The brand had served more than six million eggs since its founding, according to IMAGES RetailME.

A Diaspora Success Story

Meherish's trajectory mirrored that of many Indian entrepreneurs who arrived in the Gulf during the region's construction boom of the 1980s and gradually built business empires from modest beginnings. His insistence on sourcing fresh eggs daily from a local poultry farm — paying a 30 per cent premium over cheaper suppliers — reflected a business philosophy rooted in quality over margins.

The chain's approach to people management was equally deliberate. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Meherish insisted on maintaining staff salaries at full levels, according to Nakul. The restaurant closed every Monday so all employees could rest simultaneously, rather than using a rotation system. Staff received competitive salaries, accommodation, food, and incentives such as movie tickets.

What Comes Next

Future Plans for Raju Omlet
›Expansion into Abu Dhabi and GCC markets.
›Franchise outlets planned for Oman and Bahrain.
›Partnerships with global companies for menu items.

Prior to Meherish's death, Raju Omlet had announced plans to expand into Abu Dhabi and other GCC markets, with franchise outlets planned for Oman and Bahrain over the following two to three years. The brand had also partnered with global companies including Hellmann's Arabia for collaborative menu items. Nakul Meherish, who has been running day-to-day operations, is expected to continue leading the business.

The Dubai Indian community's response to the news, reflected in tributes across social media and industry publications, underscored the degree to which Raju Omlet had become part of the city's cultural fabric — a place where the humble egg, prepared in dozens of ways, connected expatriates to the street-food memories of home.
